tier_reason: The 1.86x (Akka) and 1.42x (CAF) figures of the ACM TACO 2023 paper (DOI 10.1145/3617687, arXiv 2301.02444) were seen only in WebSearch snippets; arXiv, par.nsf.gov, cfaed.tu-dresden.de, ar5iv and deepai were all unreachable, and the public harness (lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca runner/ and Cpp/Savina/src, CAF sources in lf-lang/savina) holds no results, CPU model or compiler, so snippet-only paper numbers stay C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper flags not seen. From the public build sources: the LF C++ benchmarks declare target Cpp { build-type: Release, no-runtime-validation: true, fast: true } (Cpp/Savina/src/micro/PingPong.lf), i.e. CMake Release (-O3 -DNDEBUG); the CAF baseline programs (lf-lang/savina CMakeLists.txt) and CAF 0.16.5 itself both default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g level) and the README build commands pass no build type, so a build that follows the README compares LF at -O3 against CAF at -O2. Compiler and version not stated.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the TACO 2023 paper and its artifact data were not opened (arXiv, par.nsf.gov, cfaed.tu-dresden.de, ar5iv and deepai unreachable), so tier C; snippets agree on 1.86x over Akka and 1.42x over CAF but give no thread count, CPU or aggregation method, and the '20 threads' setting, CAF 0.17.6, Akka 2.6.17 and i9-10900K details could not be confirmed (the benchmark README names CAF 0.16.5). Snippets also say only 22 of the 30 Savina benchmarks were ported to the LF C++ target: benchmarks needing dynamic actor creation (Fork Join creation, Fibonacci, Quicksort and others), A*-Search and Logistic Map Series (whose CAF version uses a blocking call) are excluded, so the suite average covers only benchmarks LF can express with a static reactor graph. Same-opt-level problem in the public sources: LF benchmarks build with build-type Release (-O3) plus no-runtime-validation, while the lf-lang/savina CAF programs and CAF 0.16.5 default to RelWithDebInfo (-O2) and the README passes no build type; whether the paper overrode this is unknown. The LF ports restructure the Savina programs into reactors with fixed connections (PingPong breaks its causality loop with a logical action), so the work is equivalent but not line-for-line identical to the CAF and Akka versions. The paper's authors built both sides. Both sides are C++ (LF generates C++ against the reactor-cpp runtime), so the win is a runtime and programming-model result, not a code-generation one; the paper also reports LF behind CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring and behind Akka on Counting and Big (snippet). The benchmark repo has no LICENSE file; the lingua-franca repo is BSD-2-Clause.
corrections.why_faster: Runtime and programming model, not codegen: LF programs have a statically known reactor graph that the reactor-cpp runtime schedules deterministically by tag and level, instead of CAF's dynamic per-actor mailboxes; the paper's own attribution was not readable (snippet only). Part of the gap may come from the public build defaults (LF -O3 against CAF -O2).

notes: Kept at C: numbers from TACO 2023 snippets only, benchmark_url set to the arXiv abstract (not opened, egress blocked). Shortcomings to record: snippet-only numbers; only 22 of 30 Savina benchmarks (dynamic-creation ones excluded); public build defaults put CAF at RelWithDebInfo -O2 against LF Release -O3 (same_opt_level false); win comes from the C++ reactor runtime, not the language's codegen.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: the hyper-threaded chart in the PDF is Figure 8 of the peer-reviewed AGERE! 2015 paper 'Deny Capabilities for Safe, Fast Actors' (author copy docs/media/papers/fast-cheap.pdf in ponylang-website), which states the benchmarks come from the CAF team's suite (github.com/actor-framework/benchmarks) and plots the average of 100 runs; CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated anywhere, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Read off the charts (approximate, ratios derived from page data): at 1 core Pony 0.1.5 about 3.7 versus CAF 0.13 about 0.56 (about 6.6x) and Charm++ 6.6.1 about 0.9 (about 4x); at 16 physical cores Pony about 1.67 versus CAF about 0.27 (about 6x); at 32 physical cores Pony about 1.62 versus CAF about 0.2 (about 8x). Charm++ drops to about 0.15 at 2 cores and stays at or below about 0.13 after that; Erlang OTP 17 falls below 0.1 from about 15 cores; Scala/Akka stays near 0.02 at every core count. With hyper-threading (also Figure 8 of the AGERE! 2015 paper) Pony is about 1.48 against CAF about 0.15-0.2 at 64 threads (roughly 7-10x). Every system, Pony included, loses speed as cores are added (Pony falls from 3.7 at 1 core to about 1.8 at 4), since all senders target one mailbox.
corrections.workload: Mailbox performance benchmark from the CAF benchmark suite: N sender actors each send M payload-free messages to one counting receiver, 100,000,000 messages in total (N/M split not stated). Pony side: examples/mailbox/main.pony (tag 0.1.7; now examples/actors/mailbox), Mailer actors each calling receiver.pong() M times; CAF side: src/caf/mailbox_performance.cpp in actor-framework/benchmarks. Plotted as speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core against physical cores (1-32) and against 32 physical cores with hyper-threading (up to 64 threads).
corrections.caveats: Charts only: the website PDF (6 pages, gnuplot, created 2015-07-06) and the AGERE! 2015 paper (HT chart only, Figure 8) have no tables, so all figures are read off the plots and are approximate. The paper says results are the average of 100 runs normalised to Erlang on one core, and that the benchmark implementations come from the CAF suite, written by programmers expert in each system (the CAF team for CAF). Neither source names the CPU (only '32 physical cores with HT'), compiler, optimisation flags or variance. The CAF-side build type used in 2015 could not be recovered: the suite's history before today is not browsable, and its current CMakeLists sets Erlang +native/hipe o3 and Charm++ -O3 but no C++ build type. The March 2015 tech-report version (fast-cheap-with-proof.pdf) ran an execution-time version on a 12-core 2.3 GHz Opteron 6338P; those are different runs. The versions are about a decade old (Pony 0.1.5, CAF 0.13, Charm++ 6.6.1, Erlang OTP 17, Scala 2.11.6 Akka; ponyc is now at 0.75.0 and CAF at 1.x), so the ratio may not hold today. CAF 0.13 at 1 core (about 0.56) is slower than both Erlang (1.0) and Charm++ (about 0.9) here, so the C++ baseline is a weak spot of CAF 0.13 under a contended mailbox, not tuned hand-written C++. Both papers are by the Pony authors (Causality and Imperial College). The same PDF and paper show a loss: on 'Creating 1,048,576 actors' CAF overtakes Pony beyond about 10 physical cores (about 17 versus 9 at 32 cores), so this is a per-benchmark win. The Pony runtime (libponyrt) is written in C. www.ponylang.io and a later Pony 0.26.0 versus CAF 0.16.3 run on doc.ic.ac.uk/~scb12/pony.html were blocked here and are not used.
corrections.why_faster: Runtime, not codegen: the paper credits Pony's own runtime (scheduler, memory allocator, garbage collector and message queues, written in C in libponyrt) without a per-mechanism breakdown. In the sources a Pony behaviour call is a typed asynchronous send dispatched by message id, while the CAF receiver matches each type-erased msg_atom message against its behavior at run time.

notes: Upgraded to B on the peer-reviewed AGERE! 2015 paper (same chart as Figure 8, CAF team's benchmark suite, 100-run average); CPU, compiler and flags missing. Pony and CAF programs do the same work (N senders, M empty messages, one counting receiver). Shortcomings: decade-old versions; CAF 0.13 slower than Erlang at 1 core, so a weak baseline; build flags unknown (same_opt_level null); first-party authors; the win is from Pony's C runtime; Pony loses actor creation to CAF.

tier_reason: The hyper-threaded chart is Figure 9 of the peer-reviewed AGERE! 2015 paper (author copy docs/media/papers/fast-cheap.pdf), which on its own would give B. It stays C because the public Pony program does less work than the CAF suite's mixed_case: Pony builds each ring once and discards the factorisation result, while CAF rebuilds every ring on each repetition and sends checked results to a supervisor. CPU, compiler and flags are also unstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Read off the charts (approximate, ratios derived from page data): at 1 core Pony 0.1.5 about 2.2 versus CAF 0.13 about 0.5 (about 4x); at 16 physical cores Pony about 29 versus CAF about 8 (about 3.6x); at 32 physical cores Pony about 48 versus CAF about 16 (about 3.0x), with Erlang OTP 17 about 19, Scala/Akka about 13.5 and Charm++ 6.6.1 about 9. With hyper-threading (also Figure 9 of the AGERE! 2015 paper) Pony is about 62 at 64 threads, against CAF at about 26-27 over 56-63 threads and about 30 at its final 64-thread point (about 2.1-2.4x), Erlang about 24 and Akka about 25.
corrections.workload: Mixed case ('Message ring + factorisation') from the CAF benchmark suite: rings of actors pass a token while a worker factorises 86028157 x 329545133 by trial division on each repetition. Pony side: examples/mixed/main.pony (tag 0.1.7; now examples/actors/mixed) with defaults of 20 rings of 50 actors, 10,000 laps and 5 repetitions. CAF side: src/caf/mixed_case.cpp in actor-framework/benchmarks. The run parameters behind the charts are not stated. Plotted as speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core against physical cores (1-32) and against 32 physical cores with hyper-threading (up to 64 threads).
corrections.caveats: Unequal work between implementations: in the public Pony program (unchanged from tag 0.1.7 to today) each Ring master builds its ring once and reuses it across all repetitions, spawns a fresh Worker actor per repetition, and computes but never uses the factorisation result (the 'correct' flag is dropped; no message, no check). The CAF suite's mixed_case.cpp (current version; the 2015 CAF 0.13 version could not be retrieved) spawns a new ring of ring_size-1 actors on every repetition while the old links quit, factorises in one detached (own-thread) worker per ring, and sends every factor vector to a supervisor that checks it. Pony therefore skips ring re-creation and the result messages that CAF pays for. Charts only: the website PDF (gnuplot, created 2015-07-06) and the paper have no tables, so figures are approximate. The paper gives 100-run averages but no CPU model (only '32 physical cores with HT'), compiler, flags or variance, and the CAF build type is unknown. Versions are about a decade old (Pony 0.1.5, CAF 0.13, Charm++ 6.6.1, Erlang OTP 17, Scala 2.11.6 Akka). On the physical-core chart Erlang OTP 17 beats CAF at every core count (about 19 versus 16 at 32 cores); with HT, CAF passes Erlang at about 48 threads and ends ahead (about 30 versus 24 at 64). So CAF 0.13 is a weak baseline here, and the Pony gap says more about CAF's scaling and the unequal work than about the language. Both papers are by the Pony authors. The same sources show CAF beating Pony on actor creation beyond about 10 physical cores. The Pony runtime (libponyrt) is written in C. www.ponylang.io and doc.ic.ac.uk/~scb12/pony.html were blocked and are not used.
corrections.why_faster: Mostly the runtime and the benchmark: the paper credits Pony's own runtime (C scheduler, allocator, GC and message queues in libponyrt), and the Pony program does less work than CAF's mixed_case (no per-repetition ring re-creation, no factor-result messages to a supervisor). The factorisation loop itself is the same trial division on both sides.

notes: Kept at C. The peer-reviewed AGERE! 2015 paper (Figure 9) carries the chart, but the Pony and CAF programs do unequal work: Pony skips ring re-creation per repetition and drops the factorisation result. The 64-thread figure was corrected: CAF is about 30 at its last point, so the gap is about 2.1x there, not 2.4x. Erlang does not merely reach parity; CAF overtakes it near 48 threads. Shortcomings: unequal work (same_algorithm false), flags and CPU unknown, decade-old versions, weak CAF 0.13 baseline, first-party authors.
